newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Beseiged tourists emerge after Phnom Penh battle.
newsitem.headline: Beseiged tourists emerge after Phnom Penh battle.

text.p: Hundreds of foreign tourists emerged from their hotels in downtown Phnom Penh on Monday after being besieged over the weekend by battles raging in the streets.
But embassies in the capital warned their nationals to exercise caution as soldiers, some of them drunk and firing shots in the air, looted shops and held up tourists at gunpoint.
"I'm not sure it's all over. This is not a bad hotel to stay, but now I just want to get out of here," said tourist Maxine Center of Atlanta, Georgia.

Wheelchair-bound Center was a member of a 30-strong party of Americans in their 50s and 60s from the Seventh Day Adventist Church visiting tourist sites and aid projects in Cambodia for the Adventist Development Relief Association.

The group was to visit the temples of Angkor Wat in northern Cambodia on Sunday but found themselves trapped downtown in the luxurious Juliana Hotel anxiously watching Cable News Network for developments as explosions rocked the streets.
Fighting began on Saturday and continued throughout the weekend as troops loyal to the rival co-prime ministers battled for power in the capital.
The shelling eased by Monday, when Second Prime Minister Hun Sen appeared to have taken control of Phnom Penh from forces loyal to First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh.

Joyce McCallum, 39, from Glasgow, Scotland, was also trapped in the Juliana with her husband and two children. But she said she had no intention of leaving Cambodia and planned to stay with friends in a nearby provincial town.
"I'm not afraid. I'm a barmaid and it sometimes gets pretty rough at night in Glasgow," she said.
But another British national working in Phnom Penh who ventured out on Saturday night said he had been held up at gunpoint by soldiers and robbed of his camera and mobile phone.
Guests were also trapped in their hotels by a curfew imposed between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. (1300 to 2300 GMT) by municipal authorities since Saturday night.
One American said she slept on a mattress on the floor of the Cambodiana hotel along with a large group of other Americans on Sunday night.
On Saturday, police closed down a July 4 weekend U.S. Independence Day party being held on the bank of the Tonle Sap river as fighting broke out in various parts of the city.
Phnom Penh's airport was still closed on Monday with its terminal gutted after soldiers looted its shops and lounges. No planes have been able to land or take off from the airport since Saturday.
